A sequoia is a type of enormous, ancient, cone-bearing tree native to the western United States, especially California. These are not just large trees — they are among the most massive and oldest living things that have ever existed on Earth. The word is most often used to refer to one of two closely related species, and to truly understand what "sequoia" means, you need to know both.

Giant Sequoia is the more famous of the two, and when most people say "sequoia," this is what they mean. It holds the title of the largest tree on Earth by volume — meaning the sheer amount of wood packed into a single tree. It grows in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California, at fairly high altitudes, in clusters called groves. Its trunk at the base can be wider than a two-lane road, and it can tower over 300 feet (about 90 meters) into the sky. The single most famous individual is a tree called General Sherman, located in Sequoia National Park, California. It is the largest known living tree on the planet by volume, estimated to contain enough wood to build dozens of average-sized houses.

Coast Redwood is the second species. Strictly speaking, in scientific classification, this is the true sequoia — the genus Sequoia in botany technically refers only to this species. It holds a different record: it is the tallest tree species on Earth. The tallest known individual, called Hyperion, stands at roughly 380 feet (about 116 meters) — taller than a 35-story skyscraper. Unlike the giant sequoia, it grows in a narrow strip along the Pacific Coast, from southern Oregon down to central California, in foggy, wet conditions.

So in everyday English, "sequoia" loosely covers both species, but most commonly refers to the giant sequoia. Technically, the giant sequoia belongs to a closely related but separate scientific genus called Sequoiadendron. Both belong to the same broader family as cypresses.

Both sequoias are evergreen, which means they stay green all year round and do not shed their leaves in autumn the way oaks or maples do. Their leaves are small, needle-like or scale-like, and not particularly striking — the tree's glory is almost entirely in its sheer size and age.

The most visually striking feature of a sequoia is its bark. It is thick, deeply furrowed, and a warm reddish-brown color — almost like rust. On a giant sequoia, the bark alone can be 2 to 3 feet thick. This isn't just for looks. That thick, spongy bark is a natural shield that protects the tree from fire, insects, and disease. It contains very little resin (the flammable sap found in many conifers), so even when fire does touch it, the tree is usually not seriously harmed.

The cones of a giant sequoia are surprisingly small for such a massive tree — only about the size of a chicken egg. They can hang on the tree for 20 years without opening, waiting for the right moment.

Giant sequoias regularly live for 2,000 to 3,000 years, and some have been documented at over 3,200 years old. Coast redwoods typically live over 1,000 to 2,000 years, with some exceeding 2,200 years. To put this in perspective, a sequoia tree alive today could have been a young sapling when ancient Rome was at the height of its power.

A fully grown giant sequoia can weigh over 2 million pounds (around 1,000 metric tons). Their root systems are paradoxically shallow — only about 6 to 12 feet deep — but spread outward over a very wide area, sometimes covering more than an acre. The roots of neighboring sequoias often intertwine with each other underground, which helps stabilize these enormous trees against the wind.

Giant sequoias exist in only 68 known groves, all within a relatively small region of California's Sierra Nevada mountains. They do not grow anywhere else in the wild on Earth. They need specific conditions: cold winters with heavy snowfall, warm summers, and well-drained soil.

Coast redwoods are similarly restricted, growing only along a coastal strip about 450 miles long and rarely more than 35 miles inland. This strip is kept moist and cool by ocean fog that rolls in from the Pacific, providing the humidity these trees need during California's dry summers. Without that fog, they struggle.

Both species are geographically very limited for trees of such extraordinary fame.

Sequoias have survived for millennia because they are extraordinarily well-adapted to their environment.

Fire is actually their friend. Giant sequoias have evolved to depend on fire for reproduction. Their egg-sized cones can stay sealed shut on the tree for up to 20 years. When fire sweeps through, the heat dries the cones out and causes them to open, releasing thousands of tiny seeds. At the same time, fire clears dead leaves and competing plants from the forest floor, giving the seeds bare, nutrient-rich soil to land on. Without occasional fire, giant sequoias struggle to reproduce. This is why modern fire suppression policies (putting out every fire) have actually harmed sequoia groves over the long term.

Their wood resists almost everything. Sequoia wood is naturally loaded with compounds called tannins that make it deeply resistant to rot, fungi, insects, and decay. A fallen sequoia log can sit on the forest floor for hundreds of years before it fully decomposes. This resistance is part of why living trees can survive for thousands of years.

They drink enormous amounts of water. A large coast redwood can absorb hundreds of gallons of water per day. They pull water both from the soil through their roots and directly from the fog through their leaves — a rare ability called foliar uptake.

Both sequoia species are considered endangered by international conservation standards. Their populations have declined sharply from their historical range, primarily due to logging in the 19th and 20th centuries (which cleared vast stretches of old-growth redwood forest) and, more recently, climate change.

Severe droughts, rising temperatures, bark beetle infestations, and increasingly intense wildfires now pose serious threats. Unusually destructive fires in 2020 and 2021 killed a significant percentage of the world's remaining giant sequoias — trees that had survived for thousands of years. Scientists estimate that thousands of individual giant sequoias were killed in just those two fire seasons alone.

The good news is that large areas of sequoia habitat are protected within national and state parks, including Sequoia National Park, Kings Canyon National Park, and Redwood National and State Parks in California. Conservation efforts are ongoing, including controlled burns (deliberately set fires to manage fuel buildup) and replanting programs.

A sequoia is not just a tree — it is a living record of time. When you stand at the base of a giant sequoia and look up, you are looking at something that was alive before many of the world's great civilizations rose and fell. They have outlasted kingdoms, ice ages, and centuries of human history. Their existence is a reminder of how brief a human lifetime is in the context of the natural world, and why protecting them matters so much.
